section_summary: This section contains U.S. State Department correspondence, diplomatic despatches, intelligence memoranda, cross-reference sheets, and press translations concerning prominent Japanese statesmen, diplomats, and political figures between 1931 and 1939. Major subjects include Foreign Minister Koki Hirota's early career under Enjiro Yamaza, academic queries regarding international jurist Sakutaro Tachi and a biography of Count Takaaki Kato, biographical assessments of Yosuke Matsuoka and Marquis Koichi Kido, and official condolences for departed leaders such as Yuko Hamaguchi, Masanao Hanihara, and Gonnohyoe Yamamoto. A substantial portion is devoted to the surge of right-wing terrorism in 1932, specifically detailed reporting on the assassinations of Junnosuke Inouye, Baron Takuma Dan, and Prime Minister Tsuyoshi Inukai during the May 15th Incident, analyzing the rise of military influence and reactionary nationalism.

subfiles.about: Transmits a translation of Foreign Minister Koki Hirota's magazine article recalling his mentor Enjiro Yamaza and his entry into diplomacy.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew transmits an English translation by Language Attaché John M. Allison of an article by Foreign Minister Koki Hirota published in the January issue of Hinode. Hirota recounts his introduction to diplomacy through nationalist leader Mitsuru Toyama and veteran diplomat Enjiro Yamaza. He describes student intelligence missions to Manchuria and Matsuyama during the Russo-Japanese War, Yamaza's shrewd conduct following the Portsmouth Peace Treaty, and their service together in London. Grew notes the text provides valuable insight into Hirota's personal background and character.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 619: Transmitting Translation of Article in January Number of HINODE by the Foreign Minister, Mr. Koki Hirota

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet indexing a Tokyo despatch concerning the death of Count Gonnohyoe Yamamoto.
subfiles.summary: This State Department document file note indexes Despatch No. 656 from Ambassador Grew dated January 9, 1934. It records the death of Admiral Count Gonnohyoe Yamamoto in Tokyo on December 8, 1933, at the age of 81. The cross-reference directs researchers to the main political report file 894.00 P.R./73.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Despatch No. 656 Regarding Death of Count Yamamoto

subfiles.about: Biographical obituary notice reporting the death and public career of Admiral Count Gonnohyoe Yamamoto.
subfiles.summary: This brief report section details the passing of Admiral Count Gonnohyoe Yamamoto on December 8 in Tokyo at age 81. It notes his historical role as a surviving participant of the Meiji Restoration, his appointment as Navy Minister in 1898, and his two terms as Prime Minister in 1913 and September 1923. His second premiership is highlighted for undertaking post-earthquake reconstruction following the Great Kanto Earthquake.
subfiles.title: Report Excerpt: Death of Count Yamamoto

subfiles.about: Internal linguistic note explaining that 'Tatsa' is phonologically impossible in the Japanese language.
subfiles.summary: An officer in the Division of Far Eastern Affairs provides a short linguistic memorandum concerning a queried Japanese author's name. The note clarifies that 'Tatsa' cannot be a valid Japanese name because the consonant combination 'ts' is invariably followed by the vowel 'u'. This linguistic correction helped identify Dr. Sakutaro Tachi.
subfiles.title: FE Memorandum: Transliteration of Japanese Names ('Tatsa')

subfiles.about: Departmental memorandum identifying 'Tatsa Taro' as Dr. Sakutaro Tachi and describing his prominent international law publications.
subfiles.summary: The Division of Far Eastern Affairs advises Stanley K. Hornbeck that Professor Rogers' inquiry almost certainly refers to Dr. Sakutaro Tachi, one of Japan's preeminent authorities on international law. Tachi is identified as an emeritus professor at Tokyo Imperial University, adviser to the Foreign Office, and former delegate to the Washington Conference. The memorandum reviews Tachi's standard treatises on the laws of peace and war and notes his recent 1934 publication on contemporary principles of international law.
subfiles.title: FE Memorandum for Dr. Hornbeck: Regarding Dr. Sakutaro Tachi

subfiles.about: Inquiry regarding a Japanese treatise on international law attributed to 'Tatsa Taro' and the possibility of translation.
subfiles.summary: James Grafton Rogers of Yale University writes to Stanley K. Hornbeck concerning a recent Japanese international law book acquired by fellow faculty member A. Whitney Griswold. The volume, titled in translation 'Theory of International Law Today' and attributed to 'Tatsa Taro', addresses legal rationales for Japanese foreign policy, the Manchukuo affair, the Lytton Report, and major multilateral treaties. Rogers inquires whether Hornbeck is familiar with the author and if English translations exist, exploring potential publication under Yale's Japanese studies program.
subfiles.title: Letter from James Grafton Rogers to Stanley K. Hornbeck: Inquiry Regarding Japanese International Law Book

subfiles.about: Identifies author 'Tatsa Taro' as Dr. Sakutaro Tachi and outlines his background and publications for Yale researchers.
subfiles.summary: Stanley K. Hornbeck replies to James Grafton Rogers, explaining that 'Tatsa Taro' is an erroneous transliteration for Dr. Sakutaro Tachi (Tachi Sakutaro). Hornbeck summarizes Dr. Tachi's distinguished career as an emeritus professor, Foreign Office adviser, and newly appointed member of the Permanent Court of Arbitration. He mentions Tachi's principal treatises and offers to consult the Tokyo Embassy or suggest academic experts at Yale and Harvard.
subfiles.title: Letter from Stanley K. Hornbeck to James Grafton Rogers: Identifying Dr. Sakutaro Tachi

subfiles.about: Follow-up letter thanking Hornbeck for identifying Dr. Tachi and deferring further translation inquiries.
subfiles.summary: James Grafton Rogers thanks Stanley K. Hornbeck for clarifying the identity of Dr. Sakutaro Tachi and his legal work. Rogers explains that the translation project forms part of a broader study plan for which he intends to seek Hornbeck's advice later in the winter. He concludes that no further diplomatic inquiries are required at present.
subfiles.title: Letter from James Grafton Rogers to Stanley K. Hornbeck: Acknowledging Information on Dr. Tachi

subfiles.about: Requests State Department assistance in translating a two-volume Japanese biography of Count Takaaki Kato.
subfiles.summary: Professor Daniel B. Carroll of the University of Vermont writes to Stanley K. Hornbeck regarding a two-volume Japanese biography of Count Takaaki Kato presented to him by Major Yoshiaki Nishi. Carroll emphasizes Kato's diplomatic significance during World War I and asks whether any personnel in the Division of Far Eastern Affairs could translate the biography into English. He notes his own inability to read Japanese and seeks practical suggestions.
subfiles.title: Letter from Daniel B. Carroll to Stanley K. Hornbeck: Request for Translation of Count Kato Biography

subfiles.about: Declines translation of Count Kato's biography by State Department staff and recommends scholarly institutions.
subfiles.summary: Stanley K. Hornbeck replies to Professor Carroll, stating that the Division's few Japanese-speaking officers are fully occupied with official duties and cannot undertake such a massive translation. He remarks that much of the biography is tailored to domestic Japanese audiences and may not warrant complete English publication. Hornbeck suggests contacting Mortimer Graves at the American Council of Learned Societies or Dr. Arthur W. Hummel at the Library of Congress for qualified translators.
subfiles.title: Letter from Stanley K. Hornbeck to Daniel B. Carroll: Translation Resources for Kato Biography

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet indexing a memorandum on prominent Japanese women in public life.
subfiles.summary: This document file note references a memorandum prepared on April 15, 1938, by Arthur R. Ringwalt of the Far Eastern Division. The underlying memorandum provides brief biographical sketches and data concerning prominent Japanese women active in public affairs. The paper is filed under decimal classification 893.44/9 and indexed under 894.44.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Memorandum Regarding Japanese Women of Prominence in Public Life

subfiles.about: Confidential memorandum assessing the personality, career, and political prospects of Yosuke Matsuoka.
subfiles.summary: Stanley K. Hornbeck submits a candid assessment of Yosuke Matsuoka to Under Secretary Sumner Welles to supplement an official biographical sketch. Hornbeck recounts Matsuoka's early upbringing in Oregon and portrays him as a brusque, hard-boiled figure resembling an American political boss. He recalls encountering Matsuoka in Chinese disguise in Peking and highlights his dramatic walkout from the League of Nations Assembly in 1933. Hornbeck expresses strong skepticism regarding Matsuoka's immediate chances for the premiership due to his lack of organized political support and the distrust of the Emperor and Prince Saionji.
subfiles.title: FE Memorandum for Mr. Welles: Assessment of Yosuke Matsuoka

subfiles.about: Cover memorandum transmitting an official biographical sketch of Yosuke Matsuoka to Under Secretary Welles.
subfiles.summary: Joseph W. Ballantine sends a concise cover memorandum to Under Secretary Sumner Welles pursuant to a morning request. The memorandum transmits an attached biographical summary outlining Yosuke Matsuoka's diplomatic, corporate, and political career.
subfiles.title: FE Note for Mr. Welles: Transmitting Biographical Sketch of Yosuke Matsuoka

subfiles.about: Biographical profile detailing the education, diplomatic posts, railway leadership, and political status of Yosuke Matsuoka.
subfiles.summary: This biographical sketch traces Yosuke Matsuoka's graduation from the University of Oregon, his service in the Japanese Foreign Service, and his rise as director and president of the South Manchuria Railway Company. It recounts his role as special representative during the 1932 Shanghai hostilities, his leadership of the Japanese delegation at Geneva, and his subsequent appointment as advisory counselor to the Cabinet. Ballantine notes that while Matsuoka clashed with army authorities and temporarily lost prominence, his outspoken character maintains his broad popular appeal.
subfiles.title: Biographical Sketch: Yosuke Matsuoka

subfiles.about: Intelligence memorandum analyzing Marquis Koichi Kido's background, political views, and suitability as Prime Minister.
subfiles.summary: Laurence E. Salisbury provides background on Marquis Koichi Kido following Ambassador Grew's report identifying him as a potential successor to Prime Minister Hiranuma. Kido is characterized as an influential Home Minister, close confidant of Prince Konoe, and a realistic moderate within the Cabinet. The memorandum reviews Kido's stance during the 1938 cabinet crisis, where he favored a swift and opportunistic conclusion to the China conflict over prolonged operations that risked embroiling Japan with Britain and the United States. Kido's past service in the Ministry of Agriculture and as Chief Secretary to the Lord Keeper of the Privy Seal is also outlined.
subfiles.title: FE Memorandum for the Secretary and Mr. Welles: Marquis Koichi Kido

subfiles.about: Official filing jacket for documents relating to the assassination of Baron Takuma Dan.
subfiles.summary: This State Department subject jacket establishes decimal file 894.44-DAN, BARON for records concerning the assassination of Baron Takuma Dan on March 5, 1932. Standard departmental filing instructions and classification markings appear on the cover.
subfiles.title: Subject File Jacket: Assassination of Baron Dan, of Japan

subfiles.about: Urgent telegram reporting the assassination of Baron Takuma Dan outside the Mitsui Bank by Goro Hishinuma.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador W. Cameron Forbes cables the Secretary of State reporting that Baron Dan was fatally shot through the right breast near the Mitsui Bank at 11:40 a.m. and died shortly thereafter. The arrested assailant is identified as 21-year-old Goro Hishinuma from Ibaraki Prefecture, the same home prefecture as the assassin of former Finance Minister Inouye. Forbes notes that police have not yet connected the killer to a specific group.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Telegram No. 91: Assassination of Baron Dan

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet for confidential despatch reporting murder details of Baron Takuma Dan.
subfiles.summary: This document file note indexes a strictly confidential despatch dated March 9, 1932, from Ambassador Forbes regarding details of the murder of Baron Dan in Tokyo. The underlying report is filed under 894.00/375.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Despatch on Murder of Baron Dan

subfiles.about: Confidential report describing the shooting of Baron Dan, rumors of a reactionary death pact, and police negligence.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Forbes provides a strictly confidential account of Baron Dan's shooting as he exited his car at the Mitsui Building. Forbes details the fatal bullet wound, Dan's frail health, and reports that the assassin used an automatic pistol originating from military sources. He describes pervasive rumors of a five-man death gang targeting prominent conservative figures, including Baron Shidehara, Count Makino, and Baron Wakatsuki. Forbes also notes fierce public and press criticism of the police for failing to neutralize known extremist bands.
subfiles.title: Letter from W. Cameron Forbes to the Secretary of State: Details of Baron Dan's Murder and Terrorist Threats

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet indexing Despatch No. 560 on the assassination of Baron Dan by Goro Hishinuma.
subfiles.summary: This document file note indexes Despatch No. 560 from Edwin L. Neville dated April 7, 1932, filed under 894.00 P.R./52. It notes the report concerns the assassination of Baron Dan on March 5 by reactionary youth Goro Hishinuma.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Despatch No. 560 on Assassination of Baron Dan

subfiles.about: Summary report on the assassination of Baron Dan, his commercial leadership, and the uncovered Blood Brotherhood conspiracy.
subfiles.summary: This report excerpt reviews the shock surrounding the murder of Baron Dr. Takuma Dan, senior managing director of Mitsui Gomei Kaisha and dean of Japanese finance. Coming shortly after the assassination of Junnosuke Inouye, the incident revealed that both killers hailed from the same Ibaraki village. Police investigations uncovered an organized Blood Brotherhood sworn to execute prominent national figures, including Baron Goh, Baron Wakatsuki, and Railway Minister Tokonami.
subfiles.title: Report Excerpt: Assassination of Baron Dan and Discovery of the Blood Brotherhood

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet indexing Despatch No. 561 regarding Baron Dan's murderer and the Blood Brotherhood League.
subfiles.summary: This document file note indexes Despatch No. 561 of April 7, 1932, from Chargé Neville, filed under confidential file 894.00/562. It confirms the report that the murderer of Baron Dan was an active member of the reactionary Blood Brotherhood League.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Despatch No. 561 on Baron Dan's Murderer and Blood Brotherhood League

subfiles.about: Departmental filing jacket for papers concerning former Prime Minister Yuko Hamaguchi.
subfiles.summary: This official jacket establishes file 894.44-HAMAGUCHI for correspondence and documents relating to former Premier Yuko Hamaguchi following his death in August 1931.
subfiles.title: Subject File Jacket: Yuko Hamaguchi, One-Time Premier of Japan

subfiles.about: Official American condolences on the death of former Japanese Prime Minister Yuko Hamaguchi.
subfiles.summary: Acting Secretary of State William R. Castle sends telegraphic condolences to Japanese Foreign Minister Baron Kijuro Shidehara upon the death of former Premier Yuko Hamaguchi. Castle conveys the sincere sympathy of the United States Government and American people, requesting that personal condolences be passed to Hamaguchi's family.
subfiles.title: Telegram from Acting Secretary of State Castle to Baron Kijuro Shidehara: Condolences on Death of Hamaguchi

subfiles.about: Telegraphic reply expressing gratitude for American condolences on the passing of former Premier Hamaguchi.
subfiles.summary: Baron Kijuro Shidehara thanks Acting Secretary of State Castle for his thoughtful message of sympathy on the death of Yuko Hamaguchi. He notes that Hamaguchi's family was deeply touched by the personal expression of condolence.
subfiles.title: Telegram from Baron Shidehara to Acting Secretary of State Castle: Acknowledging Condolences

subfiles.about: Appreciation from the Hamaguchi family for U.S. personal condolences.
subfiles.summary: The family of former Premier Yuko Hamaguchi sends a telegram to Acting Secretary Castle conveying their heartfelt thanks for the personal condolences delivered via Foreign Minister Shidehara.
subfiles.title: Telegram from Hamaguchi Family to Acting Secretary of State: Expression of Thanks

subfiles.about: Filing jacket for documents concerning former Ambassador Masanao Hanihara.
subfiles.summary: This jacket opens file 894.44-HANIHARA to preserve State Department correspondence regarding the death and funeral of former Japanese Ambassador to the United States Masanao Hanihara.
subfiles.title: Subject File Jacket: Hanihara - Japan

subfiles.about: Reports the death of Masanao Hanihara, former Japanese Ambassador to the United States.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew informs the Secretary of State that Masanao Hanihara, former Japanese Ambassador in Washington, died on December 20. Grew reports his intention to attend the funeral on Sunday and send an official floral wreath from the Embassy.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Telegram No. 281: Death of Masanao Hanihara

subfiles.about: Army radiogram requesting official transmission of condolences from General Frank McCoy to Hanihara's widow.
subfiles.summary: Major General Frank McCoy sends a radiogram via the War Department Message Center to the Far Eastern Division. He asks the Department to convey his deep sympathy to the widow of his longtime friend Hanihara in the most appropriate manner, offering to cover cable transmission costs.
subfiles.title: Radiogram from Major General Frank McCoy to Division of Far Eastern Affairs: Condolences for Madame Hanihara

subfiles.about: Instructs American Embassy Tokyo to convey General McCoy's condolences to Madame Hanihara.
subfiles.summary: The Department of State instructs the American Embassy in Tokyo to deliver Major General Frank McCoy's personal message of deep sympathy to the widow of former Ambassador Hanihara.
subfiles.title: State Department Telegram No. 214 to Tokyo: Transmitting General McCoy's Message

subfiles.about: Informs General McCoy that his message of sympathy has been telegraphed to Ambassador Grew in Tokyo.
subfiles.summary: Stanley K. Hornbeck acknowledges General McCoy's radiogram concerning Hanihara's passing. Hornbeck confirms that the Department has telegraphed Ambassador Grew in Tokyo to deliver McCoy's condolences to Madame Hanihara and notes that cable charges will be billed later.
subfiles.title: Letter from Stanley K. Hornbeck to Major General Frank McCoy: Condolences Transmission

subfiles.about: Advises Tokyo Embassy that Under Secretary Phillips is writing personal condolences to the Japanese Ambassador in Washington.
subfiles.summary: The Department of State cables Ambassador Grew in Tokyo referencing his report on Hanihara's death. The telegram advises that Under Secretary Phillips is sending a personal letter of sympathy to Japanese Ambassador Saito in Washington to be relayed to the Hanihara family.
subfiles.title: State Department Telegram No. 213 to Tokyo: Condolences Letter from Under Secretary Phillips

subfiles.about: Official letter of condolence on the death of former Ambassador Masanao Hanihara.
subfiles.summary: Under Secretary William Phillips expresses profound regret to Ambassador Hirosi Saito upon the passing of Saito's predecessor, Masanao Hanihara. Phillips recalls his pleasant association with Hanihara in Washington, praises his personality and intellect, and asks that condolences from himself and his colleagues be conveyed to Hanihara's family.
subfiles.title: Letter from Under Secretary William Phillips to Ambassador Hirosi Saito: Condolences on Masanao Hanihara

subfiles.about: Diplomatic note thanking Under Secretary Phillips for condolences on the death of Masanao Hanihara.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Hirosi Saito writes to Under Secretary Phillips expressing sincere gratitude for his letter of sympathy regarding Masanao Hanihara. Saito confirms that he promptly telegraphed the condolences to Hanihara's bereaved family in Japan.
subfiles.title: Letter from Ambassador Hirosi Saito to Under Secretary William Phillips: Acknowledging Condolences

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet indexing a report on the assassination of former Finance Minister Junnosuke Inouye.
subfiles.summary: This document file note indexes a despatch from Ambassador Forbes filed under 894.00 P.R./51. It concerns the political assassination of Junnosuke Inouye, prominent Minseito party leader and two-time Finance Minister.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Despatch on Assassination of Junnosuke Inouye

subfiles.about: Account of the assassination of Junnosuke Inouye and commentary on Japanese tolerance toward political violence.
subfiles.summary: This report excerpt details the fatal shooting of Junnosuke Inouye by a young reactionary as Inouye arrived for a political campaign meeting on February 9. The report highlights Inouye's central role in Minseito economic policy and compares the incident to the past murders of Prime Ministers Takashi Hara and Yuko Hamaguchi. It observes a disturbing societal tolerance in Japan for crimes committed from perceived patriotic motives, noting lenient penalties and delayed justice for political assassins.
subfiles.title: Report Excerpt: Assassination of Mr. Junnosuke Inouye

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet indexing Telegram No. 126 reporting the critical shooting of Prime Minister Ki Inukai.
subfiles.summary: This document file note indexes Tokyo Telegram No. 126 of May 15, 1932, filed under 894.00/388. It records the armed attack on Prime Minister Ki (Tsuyoshi) Inukai, reporting him critically wounded.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Telegram No. 126 on Attack on Prime Minister Inukai

subfiles.about: Initial urgent telegram reporting the armed attacks of the May 15th Incident and the critical wounding of Premier Inukai.
subfiles.summary: Chargé Edwin L. Neville reports that Prime Minister Inukai was critically wounded by gunfire early that evening. Coordinated attacks were simultaneously staged against Count Makino's residence, the Metropolitan Police Office, and Seiyukai party headquarters by men in military and naval uniforms traveling in automobiles. Neville reports that eighteen attackers surrendered, styling themselves members of a young officers' association opposed to governmental corruption and capitalism, though the city remains quiet without anti-foreign agitation.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Telegram No. 126: Armed Assaults and Shooting of Prime Minister Inukai

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet indexing Despatch No. 623 summarizing events following Premier Inukai's assassination.
subfiles.summary: This document file note indexes Tokyo Despatch No. 623 of May 20, 1932, filed under 894.00/412. It summarizes political developments and government resignations following Premier Inukai's assassination.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Despatch No. 623 Summarizing May 15-19 Events

subfiles.about: Detailed narrative of the May 15th Incident attacks, cabinet resignation under Takahashi, and political maneuvering for a successor cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Chargé Neville provides a chronological narrative of the May 15 incident, in which Premier Inukai was assassinated by eleven army cadets and six naval officers while accompanying attacks targeted police headquarters, banks, and power stations. The Inukai Cabinet resigned under temporary Premier Takahashi, while Seiyukai leaders selected Home Minister Kisaburo Suzuki as party head. Neville describes intense behind-the-scenes friction between military leaders led by General Sadao Araki and political party leaders, alongside the arrival of Prince Saionji to advise the Emperor on forming a new government.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 623: Summary of Events - May 15th-19th

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet indexing Despatch No. 624 analyzing causes and consequences of Premier Inukai's assassination.
subfiles.summary: This document file note indexes Tokyo Despatch No. 624 of May 20, 1932, filed under 894.00/413. It records Neville's comprehensive analysis of the causes, domestic results, and international repercussions of Inukai's murder.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Despatch No. 624 on Repercussions of Inukai Assassination

subfiles.about: Comprehensive analytical despatch and press editorial translations examining the May 15th Incident, military dominance, and constitutional crisis.
subfiles.summary: Chargé Neville offers an in-depth political and psychological analysis of the May 15th Incident, attributing the violence to traditional samurai notions of sacrificial protest against perceived corruption in parliamentary politics, capitalist exploitation, and agrarian distress. He traces ideological links to the Mito patriotic school (Aikyojiku) and the Blood Brotherhood, noting the simultaneous murder of informant Nishida and attempted electrical sabotage. Neville evaluates the Army's four conditions for any future government, concluding that Japan is shifting toward military-dominated state socialism under imperial authority rather than Western-style fascism. Enclosures include translated editorials from the Tokyo Asahi and Tokyo Hochi condemning direct action while acknowledging deep public dissatisfaction with political parties and corporate financiers.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 624: Analysis of Causes, Results and Repercussions of the May 15th Incident, with Press Translations

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet indexing Berlin Despatch No. 1738 on German press commentary regarding Inukai's assassination.
subfiles.summary: This document file note indexes Berlin Despatch No. 1738 of May 23, 1932, filed under 894.00/414. It cross-references Ambassador Sackett's report on German press coverage of Premier Inukai's assassination.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Despatch No. 1738 on German Newspaper Comment on Inukai's Murder

subfiles.about: Surveys German newspaper reactions to Premier Inukai's assassination and its geopolitical implications for Soviet and Pacific affairs.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Frederic M. Sackett reviews wide-ranging German editorial reactions to the assassination of Premier Inukai by radical military officers. German commentators unanimously foresaw heightened tension between Japan and the Soviet Union, identifying the assassins with extreme nationalism and anti-capitalism. Sackett analyzes perspectives from publications including the semi-official Deutsche Diplomatisch-Politische Korrespondenz, the Nazi organ Völkischer Beobachter, Goebbels's Der Angriff, Hugenberg's Lokalanzeiger, the Berliner Börsen-Zeitung, and the Berliner Tageblatt, emphasizing discussions of a Japanese Monroe Doctrine in Manchuria and potential American-Soviet diplomatic rapprochement.
subfiles.title: Berlin Despatch No. 1738: German Press Reaction to the Assassination of Premier Inukai
